title: A scale on a slope
hook: Your bathroom scale reads 70 kg on the floor. What does it read on a ramp?

knows: a bathroom scale reads your weight on the floor
a scale's reading changes with acceleration (elevator-scale, apparent weight)
doesNotKnow: that a scale measures only the push straight into its surface, which on a slope is m g cos θ
that the rest of your weight pulls you along the slope and is held by friction

misconception: A scale always reads your full weight, whatever it is resting on.
objective: The learner can explain that on a slope a scale reads only the part of the weight pushing straight into it (m g cos θ), so 70 kg reads 60.6 kg at 30°, while the along-slope part is held by friction.

claims.text: On a slope the weight splits into a part straight into the surface, N = m g cos θ, and a part along the slope, m g sin θ, which friction (or a stop) balances when the person is at rest (stage: the weight arrow split into 'into the ramp' and 'along the ramp'; caption 'At rest, not slipping.'; reveal: 'On a slope your weight splits in two: part presses into the scale (the arrow into the ramp), and part pulls you down the slope, held by friction. The steeper the slope, the smaller the push into it').
claims.source: Newton's second law with a = 0, resolved perpendicular and parallel to the incline. artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r4/check.mjs (block '64 scale-on-a-slope': frictionNeeded_N 343 at 30°, muMin 0.577; 595 N and 1.732 at 60°). Halliday, Resnick and Walker, Fundamentals of Physics, chapter on Newton's laws (inclined planes). Brief #66 claim 1.

claims.text: A 70 kg person's scale reads 70.0 kg flat, 60.6 kg at 30° and 35.0 kg at 60° (reading = m cos θ, the normal force shown as N/g) (stage: the scale display and Seen row '30°: 60.6 kg · 60°: 35.0 kg · flat: 70.0 kg'; reveal: 'On the 30° ramp your scale read 60.6 kg, and at 60° only 35.0 kg, though you still weighed 70 kg').
claims.source: 70 cos 30° = 60.62; 70 cos 60° = 35.00. artifacts/scratch/cm-physics-r4/check.mjs (reads_kg 70, 60.6, 35). Demo.tsx reads(). Brief #66 claim 2.

claims.text: A bathroom scale measures the force perpendicular to its platform (reveal: 'A scale measures only the push straight into its surface').
claims.source: A spring or load cell under the platform responds to the force pressing the platform toward its base; the scale's display converts that force to kg by dividing by g. Brief #66 claim 3 (textbook; idealisation stated in c4).

claims.text: Idealisations: a rigid scale that measures only the perpendicular force, the person at rest, and a stop block holding the scale at 60° (a friction coefficient of at least 1.73 would be needed without it). The arrows are drawn to scale with each other (62 px for the full weight), not with the person.
claims.source: Stated assumption, brief #66 claim 4 and Check (muMin 1.732 at 60°). Demo.tsx: WLEN 62, components WLEN cos θ and WLEN sin θ. The caption 'At rest, not slipping.' and the 'stop block' label carry the assumptions on the stage.

recall.question: A crate rests on a steep ramp. Is the ramp pushing on it, straight out of its surface, with more, less or the same force as its weight?
recall.why: Only part of the weight presses into a sloping surface (m g cos θ); the rest pulls the crate along the slope and is held by friction.
